newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: First test of Boutros' UN re-election hopes Monday.
newsitem.headline: First test of Boutros' UN re-election hopes Monday.

text.p: The first test of United Nations Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's hopes for re-election and repeated United States threats to block him could come as early as next Monday, Security Council sources said on Tuesday.
This followed a private lunch attended by all 15 council members at which procedures for the election were discussed.

The sources said they agreed to hold informal consultations on Nov. 18 at which a resolution recommending Boutros-Ghali's nomination to the General Assembly could be submitted by a group from Egypt, Botswana and Guinea-Bissau, the council's three African members.

A secretary-general is elected by the 185-nation General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council whose five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- all have a veto.
It remained uncertain when a vote would be held on nominating Boutros-Ghali, regarded by council members as the only official candidate so far.

One source said some members might wish to postpone secret ballotting to allow further time for efforts to reach a compromise with the United States, which has repeatedly insisted the United Nations needs new leadership.
Ruling out any hopes of such a compromise, a U.S. official reiterated on Tuesday that "our position remains firm and is irrevocable."
Assuming the United States vetoes Boutros-Ghali when voting takes place, the door would then be opened for other names to be submitted.

Council President Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia and others have made known their preference for an African, since previous secretaries-general from other regions -- such as Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, Kurt Waldheim of Austria and U Thant of Burma -- have all had two terms in office.
By this reasoning if Boutros-Ghali, a veteran Egyptian diplomat, is denied a second term, his successor should at least also be from Africa.
Wisnumurti has said he hopes the election process can be completed before the end of November, when his month as council president expires.
In the event of a deadlock or other problems, the task of completing the ballotting could still fall to his successor, ambassador Franceso Fulci of Italy, who will preside during December.

Boutros-Ghali's current five-year term expires on Dec. 31. Among the African candidates mentioned as possible replacements are Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping; Olara Ottuno, Ugandan head of the New York-based International Peace Academy and Hamid Algabid of Niger, the head of the Islamic Conference.
